name: Jean-Paul Sartre
worldviewSummary: Sartre holds that for human beings existence precedes essence: there is no given human nature, so we are 'condemned to be free' and wholly responsible for what we make of ourselves. Denying this freedom — hiding behind roles, nature or circumstances — is bad faith.
biography: French philosopher, novelist and playwright, central figure of postwar existentialism and a politically engaged public intellectual. He declined the 1964 Nobel Prize in Literature.

concepts.description: Man first exists, encounters himself and surges up in the world, and defines himself afterwards; there is no human nature fixed in advance.
Self-deception in which one denies one's freedom, as in the café waiter who plays at being a waiter as though it were his fixed essence.
We did not create ourselves, yet once thrown into the world we are responsible for everything we do.

positions.statement: In choosing for ourselves we choose for all humanity, because each choice affirms an image of what a human being ought to be.
There is no determinism to hide behind; passions, circumstances or human nature cannot serve as excuses for our choices.
No general morality can tell us what to do in concrete situations — illustrated by the student torn between his mother and joining the Free French; he must invent his choice.

relations.note: Lifelong intellectual partners in French existentialism.
